prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, in which magic-wavelength trapping of many neutral atoms made precision time and frequency measurement possible at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: After the full round-1 exchange I keep the lattice clock at the head of my configuration, and I now hold it for scientific reasons and not only because it unites the committee. Six members reach it from different starting points: Lindroth and Kroll for the Lamb-Dicke and magic-wavelength argument, Johansson for the many-body and redshift physics, Olsson and Mehlig for attribution and maturity. Danielsson and Eriksson, who prefer other candidates, both name it as the cleaner attribution. The physics is not in dispute. Katori's magic wavelength removes the conflict between tight confinement and a narrow transition, so a very large number of neutral atoms can be interrogated at once; Ye's group drove that to about 1e-18 and used it for centimetre-scale gravitational time dilation; JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, SYRTE and NIST now agree with one another at that level, which is the independent confirmation I ask for in any claim. The credit is two people, one originator of the scheme and one leader in demonstrated performance. A citation that says invention and realisation, and names the magic-wavelength trapping, answers the worry that it credits the whole clock community.
statement.case_against: The distinctness objection has not gone away. The committee honoured the comb in 2005 and control of single quantum systems, including ion clocks, in 2012, and a critic can say precision time has been prized twice and a third award is a successor. My answer is that the lattice scheme solved a different problem, trapping many neutral atoms without a light shift, and that no earlier prize covers it, but I accept that this is a judgement and not a proof. The second reservation is that it is a measurement invention, not a discovery from nature, and Danielsson is right that the largest scientific payoff, a redefined second, constants searches and geodesy, is still ahead. The third is credit: Lemonde, Lisdat, Ludlow, Takamoto and the ion-clock groups are outside the two names. I also record that atomic clocks are outside my expertise and the priority dates in this file are recalled and not verified, so I would want an expert evaluation of them before the final ballot.

responses.point: Lindroth argues that the lattice clock is a real conceptual step, since the magic-wavelength trap with Lamb-Dicke confinement is what separates it from a better clock, and she names the overlap with 2005 and 2012 as the main reservation while admitting she may be too fond of the field.
responses.response: I accept the conceptual argument and it is the reason I keep the clock first. I would like her to take the chair's question directly: the sentence I would defend is that the comb made optical clocks countable, the ion work showed control of a single quantum system, and the lattice scheme is the only route that combines neutral-atom numbers with ion-like freedom from Doppler and recoil shifts. If she, as the member closest to atomic structure, cannot defend that sentence, I would reconsider; if she can, I think the overlap objection is answered. I also take her disclosure seriously and treat her first place as slightly inflated, as I do my own move from IceCube.

responses.point: Danielsson prefers IceCube as a discovery handed to us by nature and says the clock, as an instrument, should wait for the SI redefinition and for the constants and dark-matter searches to deliver results.
responses.response: I share the instinct, and I ranked IceCube first in my opening ballot, so I will not wave his case away. The flux is secure and I would not call IceCube early on that basis. But my own caveats stand: confirmation is across IceCube channels and not across detectors, KM3NeT and Baikal-GVD are not yet comparable, and the three-name cut from Halzen, Karle, Spiering and the AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND lineage has no principled boundary that I can defend. The clock has the opposite profile: confirmation across five laboratories and a pair that maps on to invention and performance. I do not think waiting for the second to be redefined is a reason to wait, because the science already delivered, gravitational time dilation at centimetre scale, does not depend on that decision. I would support a request for an expert note on KM3NeT, Baikal-GVD and the pioneers, because IceCube remains a strong prize for a coming year.

responses.point: Kroll supports the clock as a new measurement technique that changes what can be observed, built on coherence and linewidth control, and discounts his own metrology bias.
responses.response: I agree, and it is the criterion I apply as an instrument builder: a technique that opens a regime nobody could reach. I agree also with his refusal to rank B020 for want of a defensible three-name credit, and with his view that a second part cannot fit the three-person limit alongside two clock laureates. I would ask him to say whether he sees any credit more complete than Katori and Ye that stays within three names, since adding Lemonde or Ludlow would put the question of who else, such as Lisdat, immediately.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers topological insulators for Kane, Mele and Molenkamp as a new class of matter confirmed by theory, transport and ARPES, accepts that the credit is not clean, and asks whether the clock is an enabling instrument or tells us something new.
responses.response: I take his question seriously and answer that the clock has told us something new: height-resolved gravitational redshift, many-body physics in the lattice, and tight bounds on drifts of constants. On B016 I accept that a prize can name a theory and a first observation without exhausting a field, but the Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposal that Molenkamp tested, with Zhang deceased, and the 2016 precedent leave a credit gap that I cannot weigh without an expert on the field. I rely on him for the physics and keep B016 as my second alternative, since his own statement calls B014 the cleaner configuration if the gap is too large.

responses.point: Johansson prefers the clock for its attribution and prior recognition while calling topological insulators conceptually deepest, and discloses his ties to circuit QED, which he has discounted.
responses.response: I value both the candour and the discounting, and it makes his support for the clock more informative, since it comes from a member who gave up his own first choice. On B009 I still see timing as the problem and not the science, given the 2025 prize, and I would not be unhappy to see the disclosure resolved by his stepping back from that candidate only. I agree with him that the citation must say invention and realisation, and I would hold to that wording in the final ballot.

uncertainties: Whether an expert on atomic clocks would accept that the lattice scheme is distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes in a single sentence.
The priority history among Katori, Ye, Lemonde, Lisdat, Ludlow, Takamoto and the ion-clock groups, which I recall but have not checked.
Whether to proceed before the formal redefinition of the second; I think the demonstrated science is sufficient but this is a judgement.
For IceCube, how much independent confirmation KM3NeT and Baikal-GVD will provide and whether any three-name credit is defensible.
My own position moved from IceCube to the clock after reading the other ballots, so some of the agreement on B014 may reflect members moving toward it and not independent convergence.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict with B014 is apparent from my profile, and atomic clocks are outside my expertise. I work in the PAMELA, Fermi-LAT and XL-Calibur collaborations, not IceCube, but KTH astroparticle physics is close to that field, so my alternative of B021 should be read with that in mind; no recusal seems required. As Chair I note that I changed my preference after reading the opening ballots and I disclose that so the committee can weigh it.
